captions.text: Recap of Part 4: embeddings let you search a handbook by meaning.
RAG cut documents into chunks, searched them, and asked the model once.
Why chunk? Because text that doesn't fit the window is cut, with no error.
Then the agent took over the search. All of those were short runs.
Today's black box: keeping a long chat inside the window.
Let's open it. But first, a chat that forgets.
Priya gives her staff number, then asks 40 handbook questions. The whole chat is sent each time.
Predict: will the assistant find the number both times?
Early on, yes. After 43 turns, it says it can't know. No error, no warning.
You can't manage what you don't measure. About four characters a token, plus a little.
It's free, with no model call. Add it up, and you know what you're sending.
How rough is it? Compare it with the model's own count, in a big window.
Within 1% on the long chats. It's a rule of thumb for English prose, so check yours.
Grow the chat. Ask for three facts, five times each. Predict: a slow fade, or a cliff?
Perfect up to 2,755 tokens.
Then 0 of 15. We sent about 5,300, and the model read about 4,000. That's the window.
The same chat at num_ctx 16384 scores 15 of 15. And Cheers survived every run.
So the rules stayed, and the oldest messages went. It keeps its manners and loses its memory.
First, stop the silence. CutWarning is a hook, and it counts what you sent.
Afterwards it compares that with what the model read. 0.9 leaves room for a rough count.
The 43-turn chat again, through an Agent, using history.
It spoke up on the real cut, and it stayed quiet at the bigger window.
If something must go, choose what. A token budget is a number you pick, below the window.
Trim pins the system message, and keeps the newest messages that fit.
Trim to 3,000 tokens. Predict: will it find the staff number now?
The budget held. The number is still gone, because old is what you told Trim to remove.
Trim gives you control, not memory.
So don't throw old messages away. Keep the newest word for word, and summarise the rest.
If there's a note already, it goes in too, so there's only ever one.
The model writes the note, and the note joins the system message.
A short test: 45 turns, five facts, five runs. Predict: which setups get all 25?
Nothing and Trim tie at 10. Both lose the three oldest facts.
A bigger window and one Summarise both get 25. It looks perfect.
Now 120 turns and twelve facts, summarised again and again. Predict: how many of 36 come back?
Look at summarise. 12 to 14 summaries, and Sent stays about 3,000. The budget held.
And it got 1 or 2 of 12 right.

captions.text: Fact by fact: 5 of 36. Only 2 notes of 36 held a personal fact.
shift passed because it's still in the chat word for word. Ten facts are simply gone.
We said: leave out handbook text. Every note is a tidy handbook summary.
Each round is a new chance to drop a fact, and a dropped fact can't come back.
Read the answers. Priya's manager is Tomasz. With the whole chat, it says so.
From the note, it names handbook managers instead. Sure, and wrong, in 3 runs of 3.
Why not a bigger window? The whole chat fits at 24,576. Window scored 22 of 36.
And both allergy passes are false. It only used cashews as an example. So 20.
Every fact was in the window. Fitting isn't the same as being used.
We tested one 7B model on one chat, three runs each. A bigger model may do better, so measure yours.

You've finished when you see 5 passed.

Trim and Summarise keep you in budget, and a short test made Summarise look perfect.
The long test didn't. Summaries lose the facts that matter.
